draft.title: Hedging and international payments
card: Hedging
Hedging cuts the risk that a change in the exchange rate will hurt a business. It is done with derivatives, which are contracts whose value comes from an underlying item such as a currency.
Forward contract
A deal to exchange currency at a rate fixed today, on a set date in the future. The business knows the amount it will get or pay, whichever way the market rate moves.
Swaps and options
A swap is an agreement to exchange currency payments with another party. An option gives the right, but not the duty, to exchange at an agreed rate.
Payment methods

A letter of credit is a bank's promise to pay the exporter once the agreed documents are shown. Payment in advance means the buyer pays before the goods are sent. Both make overseas payment safer for the exporter.
draft.remember: Hedging fixes the exchange rate risk. Letters of credit and advance payment cut the risk of not being paid.

a.q: Why would an importer use a forward contract?
opts: To fix the exchange rate for a future payment
To get a bank's promise that the goods will arrive
To make the supplier pay before the goods are sent
To raise the value of the Australian dollar
a.why: A forward contract fixes the rate today for a payment on a set future date, so the importer knows the cost. A letter of credit is the bank promise, and it deals with payment risk, not currency risk.
a.clue: Think about which risk comes from a changing exchange rate.

b.q: Jaya's Sydney firm will sell machinery to a new buyer in Chile, whom she has never dealt with. She worries the buyer might not pay. Which method best deals with this worry?
opts: A letter of credit from the buyer's bank
A forward contract on the Chilean currency
An option on the Chilean currency
A swap of currency payments with a bank
b.why: A letter of credit means a bank promises to pay once the agreed documents are shown, so Jaya does not rely on the buyer alone. A forward contract is tempting, but it only fixes the exchange rate. It does not make sure she is paid.
b.clue: Her worry is about being paid, not about the exchange rate.

a.best: To fix the exchange rate for a future payment

b.best: A letter of credit from the buyer's bank

problems.detail: The remember line says hedging 'fixes' the exchange rate risk, but the card says hedging 'cuts' it. Options and swaps do not fix a rate, and hedging reduces risk rather than removing it. It should say 'cuts' or 'reduces'.

Why (a) says 'A letter of credit is the bank promise', which links the distractor 'a bank's promise that the goods will arrive' to a letter of credit. A letter of credit is a promise to pay the exporter once the agreed documents are shown, not a promise that goods will arrive. This could teach students a wrong idea of letters of credit.

Three options are currency hedging tools and only the letter of credit is a payment method. The clue then says the worry is not about the exchange rate, so a student can pick the odd one out without knowing what a letter of credit does.

card: Hedging
Hedging cuts the risk that a change in the exchange rate will hurt a business. It is done with derivatives, which are contracts whose value comes from an underlying item such as a currency.
Forward contract

A deal to exchange currency at a rate fixed today, on a set date in the future. Both sides must go through with it, so the business knows the amount it will get or pay, whichever way the market rate moves.
Swaps and options
A swap is an agreement to exchange currency payments with another party. An option gives the right, but not the duty, to exchange at an agreed rate.
Payment methods

A letter of credit is a bank's promise to pay the exporter once the agreed documents are shown. Payment in advance means the buyer pays before the goods are sent. Both make overseas payment safer for the exporter.
proposal.remember: Hedging cuts exchange rate risk. Letters of credit and payment in advance cut the risk of not being paid.

a.q: Why would an importer use a forward contract?
opts: To lock in the exchange rate for a future payment
To have the right, but not the duty, to exchange later
To be sure the overseas supplier sends the goods
To raise the value of the Australian dollar
a.why: A forward contract fixes the rate today for a payment on a set future date, so the importer knows the cost in dollars. The right but not the duty to exchange describes an option. A forward contract binds both sides to go through with the deal.
a.clue: Does a forward contract let the business walk away?

b.q: Jaya's Sydney firm will sell machinery to a new buyer in Chile. The buyer will not pay before the machinery is shipped, and Jaya worries it might not pay at all. Which method best deals with this worry?
opts: A letter of credit from the buyer's bank
Payment in advance from the buyer
A forward contract on the Chilean peso
An option on the Chilean peso
b.why: With a letter of credit, the buyer's bank promises to pay Jaya once the agreed documents are shown, so she does not rely on the buyer alone. Payment in advance would also cut the risk, but the buyer will not pay before shipping. Forward contracts and options deal with exchange rate risk, not the risk of not being paid.
b.clue: Check what the buyer has refused to do.

a.best: To lock in the exchange rate for a future payment

b.best: A letter of credit from the buyer's bank
